edition.name: Migne, Patrologia Latina (PL 1, Paris 1844), De baptismo, via Latin Wikisource transcription
edition.witness_note: Single locked witness in repo; second witness not yet locked.

source_text: Dehinc manus imponitur, per benedictionem advocans et invitans Spiritum sanctum. Sane humano ingenio licebit spiritum in aquam arcessere et concorporationem eorum, accommodatis desuper manibus, alio spiritu tantae claritatis animare; Deo autem in suo organo non licebit per manus sanctas sublimitatem modulari spiritalem? Sed est hoc quoque de veteri sacramento, quo nepotes suos ex Joseph Ephraim et Manassem Jacob, capitibus impositis et intermutatis manibus, benedixerit, et quidem ita transversim obliquatis in se, ut Christum deformantes, jam tunc portenderent benedictionem in Christum futuram. Tunc ille sanctissimus Spiritus super emundata et benedicta corpora libens a Patre descendit, super Baptismi aquas, tanquam pristinam sedem recognoscens, conquiescit, columbae figura delapsus in Dominum, ut natura Spiritus sancti declararetur per animal simplicitatis et innocentiae, quod etiam corporaliter ipso felle careat columba. Ideoque: Estote, inquit, simplices sicut columbae, ne hoc quidem sine argumento praecedentis figurae. Quemadmodum enim post aquas diluvii, quibus iniquitas antiqua purgata est, post Baptismum (ut ita dixerim) mundi pacem coelestis irae praeco columba terris adnuntiavit dimissa ex arca, et cum olea reversa; quod signum etiam apud nationes paci praetenditur: eadem dispositione spiritalis effectus terrae, id est carni nostrae emergenti de lavacro post vetera delicta, columba sancti Spiritus advolat, pacem Dei afferens, emissa de coelis, ubi Ecclesia est arca figurata. Sed mundus rursus delinquit, quo male comparetur Baptismus diluvio. Itaque igni destinatur, sicut et homo qui post Baptismum delicta restaurat, ut hoc quoque in signum admonitionis nostrae debeat accipi.
pass_a_gloss: Then a hand is placed, through a blessing calling and inviting the Holy Spirit. Indeed, it will be permitted to human ingenuity to summon a spirit into the water and to animate their incorporation, with hands accommodated from above, with another spirit of such great clarity; but to God in His own instrument will it not be permitted through holy hands to modulate spiritual sublimity? But this is also from the old sacrament, by which Jacob blessed his grandchildren from Joseph, Ephraim and Manasseh, with hands placed on their heads and interchangeably, and indeed in such a way crosswise and obliquely in themselves, that they, deforming Christ, already then portended the blessing in Christ to come. Then that most holy Spirit willingly descends from the Father over the purified and blessed bodies, over the waters of Baptism, as if recognizing His former seat, and rests, having fallen in the form of a dove into the Lord, so that the nature of the Holy Spirit might be declared through an animal of simplicity and innocence, which dove also corporally lacks bile. And therefore: Be, He says, simple as doves, not even this without argument from the preceding figure. For just as after the waters of the flood, by which ancient iniquity was purified, after Baptism (so to speak) a dove, herald of celestial wrath, announced peace to the earth, dismissed from the ark, and with an olive branch returned; which sign is also held out to the nations for peace: by the same disposition the spiritual effect on the earth, that is, on our flesh emerging from the bath after former sins, the dove of the Holy Spirit flies, bringing the peace of God, sent from heaven, where the Church is the figurated ark. But the world again sins, by which Baptism is compared unfavorably to the flood. And so it is destined for fire, just as also the man who after Baptism restores sins, so that this also ought to be accepted as a sign of our admonition.

choices.why: accurate translation of Latin 'praeco' and 'coelestis irae'

pass_b_english: Then a hand is laid on, through a blessing calling and inviting the Holy Spirit. It will be allowed for human ingenuity to summon a spirit into water and to animate their embodiment, with hands supplied from above, with another spirit of such brilliance; but will it not be allowed to God in His own instrument, through holy hands, to modulate spiritual sublimity? This also belongs to the old sacrament, by which Jacob blessed his grandchildren from Joseph, Ephraim and Manasseh, with hands placed on their heads and crossed, and indeed in such a way crosswise and obliquely upon themselves, that they, distorting Christ, even then portended the blessing in Christ to come. Then that most holy Spirit descends willingly from the Father over the purified and blessed bodies, over the waters of Baptism, as if recognizing His former seat, and rests, having fallen in the form of a dove upon the Lord, so that the nature of the Holy Spirit might be declared through an animal of simplicity and innocence, a dove which also bodily lacks bile. And therefore: "Be simple as doves," He says, and not even this without argument from the preceding figure. For just as after the waters of the flood, by which ancient iniquity was purged, after Baptism (so to speak) a dove, herald of celestial wrath, announced peace to the earth, dismissed from the ark, and returned with an olive branch; which sign is also held out among the nations for peace: by the same disposition the spiritual effect upon the earth, that is, upon our flesh emerging from the bath after former sins, the dove of the Holy Spirit flies down, bringing the peace of God, sent from heaven, where the Church is the figured ark. But the world sins again, by which Baptism compares unfavorably to the flood. And so it is destined for fire, just as also the man who after Baptism restores sins, so that this too must be accepted as a sign of our admonition.
